cards.statement: Resource Manager folders can sit below a project in the resource hierarchy.
cards.explanation: A folder belongs under an organization or another folder. Projects can sit under folders, but they do not contain Resource Manager folders.
cards.misconception: Projects can be parents of Resource Manager folders.

cards.statement: A project IAM role can authorize creation of Cloud Identity groups.
cards.explanation: Google Workspace group permissions govern who creates Cloud Identity groups, including when creation happens in the Google Cloud console.
cards.misconception: Project IAM roles control Cloud Identity group administration.

source.title: Create and manage Google groups in the Google Cloud console

cards.statement: Google Cloud Directory Sync can provision Active Directory groups into Cloud Identity.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud Directory Sync provisions users and, optionally, groups from Active Directory into Cloud Identity or Google Workspace.

cards.statement: The gcloud services command group enables APIs for a selected Google Cloud project.
cards.explanation: The gcloud services enable command enables a named service for the current project.

cards.statement: A Cloud Monitoring metrics scope can include metrics stored in other projects.
cards.explanation: The scoping project can chart and alert on time series stored in other projects added to its metrics scope.

cards.statement: A project quota increases when a user submits its adjustment request.
cards.explanation: Cloud Quotas evaluates adjustment requests and can deny them. Submission alone does not increase the quota.
cards.misconception: Submitting a quota adjustment immediately grants the requested capacity.

cards.statement: A standalone Google Cloud organization requires a Cloud Identity account for its creation.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud creates a standalone organization for an eligible signup using a Google email address, with no Cloud Identity account required.
cards.misconception: Every organization must be backed by Cloud Identity.
cards.volatilityNote: Standalone organization signup and eligibility may evolve.

cards.statement: The gcloud compute regions list command reports machine-type availability by zone.
cards.explanation: Use gcloud compute machine-types list to check which zones support a machine type. The regions list reports regional information such as status and quotas.
cards.misconception: Listing regions also checks zonal machine-type support.

cards.statement: Cloud Asset Inventory exports asset snapshots to BigQuery for SQL analysis.
cards.explanation: An export writes the asset metadata of a project, folder or organization, as of one point in time, to a BigQuery table, where SQL queries can analyze it.

cards.statement: Workforce Identity Federation stores external users as Cloud Identity accounts.
cards.explanation: Workforce Identity Federation authenticates users through an external identity provider without synchronizing them into Cloud Identity accounts.
cards.misconception: Workforce federation provisions a Google-managed user for each external user.

cards.statement: A Cloud Billing account can collect usage charges from several projects.
cards.explanation: One Cloud Billing account accrues charges for the projects linked to it, and an account can link to multiple projects.

source.title: Enable, disable, or change billing for a project

cards.statement: A project linked to a suspended Cloud Billing account keeps billing enabled.
cards.explanation: Billing is enabled only when the linked Cloud Billing account is active and in good standing. A suspended account leaves linked projects without enabled billing.
cards.misconception: A billing-account link is sufficient even when the account is suspended.

source.title: Verify the billing status of your projects

cards.statement: Moving a project to another Cloud Billing account transfers its earlier charges.
cards.explanation: Charges incurred before a project changes billing accounts remain on its former Cloud Billing account, even if they appear in transaction history later.
cards.misconception: Relinking a project moves its previous usage charges to the new account.

source.title: Enable, disable, or change billing for a project

cards.statement: A project Owner can link the project to any Cloud Billing account.
cards.explanation: Changing a project's Cloud Billing account requires project permissions and permissions on the relevant billing accounts; project ownership alone does not authorize an arbitrary target account.
cards.misconception: Project ownership grants access to every potential billing account.

source.title: Enable, disable, or change billing for a project

cards.statement: Cloud Billing budgets accept project and service filters for cost alerts.
cards.explanation: An alerts-only budget can narrow the costs it monitors to selected projects and services.

source.title: Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts

cards.statement: A Cloud Billing budget alert can trigger from forecasted spend.
cards.explanation: Cloud Billing budget threshold rules can evaluate either actual spend or forecasted spend.

source.title: Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts

cards.statement: Cloud Billing budgets publish programmatic notifications to a configured Pub/Sub topic.
cards.explanation: Connecting a Pub/Sub topic to a Cloud Billing budget delivers programmatic budget-status notifications to that topic.

cards.statement: Standard usage cost export identifies the cost of each Compute Engine VM.
cards.explanation: The detailed usage cost export adds resource-level cost information where available. The standard usage cost export reports broader billing dimensions.
cards.misconception: Standard billing export has the same resource-level detail as detailed export.

source.title: Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery

cards.statement: Cloud Billing pricing export requires the BigQuery Data Transfer Service API.
cards.explanation: The project containing the pricing-export dataset needs the BigQuery Data Transfer Service API enabled.
cards.volatilityNote: The setup dependencies for billing exports may change.

source.title: Set up Cloud Billing data export to BigQuery

cards.statement: Cloud Billing creates the BigQuery dataset when you enable the Detailed usage cost export.
cards.explanation: For Standard and Detailed usage cost exports, you create the BigQuery dataset first and select it; Cloud Billing then creates the export tables inside it.
cards.misconception: Enabling the Detailed usage cost export also provisions its destination dataset.

source.title: Set up Cloud Billing data export to BigQuery

cards.statement: With OS Login enabled, Compute Engine accepts SSH keys stored in VM metadata.
cards.explanation: With OS Login enabled, Compute Engine uses keys associated with the user's Google identity and stops accepting SSH keys from project or instance metadata.
cards.misconception: OS Login supplements metadata-based SSH keys.

cards.statement: Compute Engine Spot VMs can run for a maximum of 24 hours.
cards.explanation: Spot VMs have no fixed maximum runtime unless you configure one. The 24-hour limit belongs to preemptible VMs.
cards.misconception: The preemptible VM runtime limit also applies to Spot VMs.

cards.statement: Regional Persistent Disk replicates a disk across two Google Cloud regions.
cards.explanation: Regional Persistent Disk replicates data between two zones within one region, protecting against a zonal failure.
cards.misconception: Regional Persistent Disk replication crosses region boundaries.

cards.statement: Google Cloud Hyperdisk lets users change provisioned performance while a volume is in use.
cards.explanation: Hyperdisk supports changing provisioned IOPS or throughput on an in-use volume, according to the Hyperdisk type.

cards.statement: GKE Autopilot requires users to create node pools before deploying workloads.
cards.explanation: GKE Autopilot manages and provisions worker nodes for deployed workloads; users do not create node pools first.
cards.misconception: Autopilot has the same user-managed node-pool setup as GKE Standard.

cards.statement: A zonal GKE cluster with nodes in several zones runs a single control plane in one zone.
cards.explanation: A zonal cluster keeps one control plane in one zone even when its nodes span several zones of the region; a regional cluster is the type that replicates the control plane across zones.

cards.statement: kubectl requires gke-gcloud-auth-plugin to authenticate to GKE clusters.
cards.explanation: GKE uses gke-gcloud-auth-plugin to provide authentication tokens to kubectl and other Kubernetes clients.

source.title: Install kubectl and configure cluster access

cards.statement: Cloud Run functions use Eventarc to receive Cloud Storage object events.
cards.explanation: Event-driven Cloud Run functions receive Cloud Storage events through Eventarc triggers.

cards.statement: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform deploys agents to user-managed GKE clusters.
cards.explanation: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is a fully managed runtime that deploys and scales agent applications while abstracting the underlying infrastructure.
cards.misconception: Using Agent Runtime means operating the agent's GKE cluster.
tags: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
cards.volatilityNote: Agent Platform runtime packaging and deployment options are evolving.

cards.statement: Cloud SQL can host MariaDB as a managed database engine.
cards.explanation: Cloud SQL offers managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server engines; MariaDB is not among its supported engines.
cards.misconception: MariaDB is a Cloud SQL engine because of its relationship to MySQL.
cards.volatilityNote: Cloud SQL's supported engine list may expand.

cards.statement: BigQuery batch load jobs ingest files stored in Cloud Storage into a table.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery batch load job reads supported source files from Cloud Storage and loads them into a BigQuery table.

cards.statement: Firestore multi-region locations place read-write replicas in separate regions.
cards.explanation: A Firestore multi-region location stores read-write replicas across regions so the database can continue serving data after a regional loss.

cards.statement: Spanner Enterprise edition provides multi-region instance configurations.
cards.explanation: Spanner multi-region instance configurations are available in Enterprise Plus edition.
cards.misconception: Spanner Enterprise includes the multi-region configurations of Enterprise Plus.
cards.volatilityNote: Spanner's edition feature matrix may change.

cards.statement: Bigtable orders rows by the lexicographic sort of their row keys.
cards.explanation: Bigtable sorts rows lexicographically by row key, so key design affects which related rows a range read reaches.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub deletes an unacknowledged message when its acknowledgment deadline expires.
cards.explanation: When an acknowledgment deadline expires, Pub/Sub attempts to redeliver the unacknowledged message.
cards.misconception: An acknowledgment deadline is a message-deletion deadline.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage Archive can retrieve objects through an offline restore job.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage Archive objects remain online and available within milliseconds; reads do not require an offline restore job.
cards.misconception: Archive objects need rehydration before they can be read.

cards.statement: Storage Transfer Service moves on-premises file data into Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: Storage Transfer Service supports transfers from on-premises storage into Cloud Storage.

cards.statement: A dual-region Cloud Storage bucket confirms uploads after replication to both regions.
cards.explanation: A successful upload confirms redundancy within the initial region. Cloud Storage replicates the object to the second region asynchronously.
cards.misconception: Successful upload means cross-region replication has already finished.

cards.statement: Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka sizes its broker count from cluster vCPU capacity.
cards.explanation: When creating a cluster, you specify total vCPU count and memory; Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka provisions the broker count from the vCPU count.
tags: Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka
cards.volatilityNote: Managed Kafka cluster-sizing behavior may evolve.

source.title: Managed Service for Apache Kafka overview

cards.statement: In Shared VPC, the shared subnets that service project VMs use belong to the service project.
cards.explanation: Shared subnets live in the host project's Shared VPC network. Service Project Admins create VMs in them, but the host project creates and owns the subnets.
cards.misconception: Service projects own the Shared VPC subnets they use.

cards.statement: VPC Network Peering can make a peer's other peers reachable through it.
cards.explanation: VPC Network Peering is non-transitive. Two networks peered with a common third network need their own connection to reach each other.
cards.misconception: Peering provides transit through a shared peer network.

cards.statement: A VPC firewall rule selects the target VM instances by matching their attached secure tag values.
cards.explanation: VPC firewall rules use network tags to select VMs. Secure tags select sources or targets in Cloud NGFW firewall policies.
cards.misconception: Secure tags target VMs in ordinary VPC firewall rules.

cards.statement: A VPC firewall rule can target VMs through their attached service account.
cards.explanation: A VPC firewall rule with target service accounts applies to VMs using a matching service account in the rule's network.

cards.statement: A VPC firewall rule can filter TCP traffic by its source port.
cards.explanation: VPC firewall rules can filter TCP traffic by destination port. Their protocol and port settings do not support source-port matching.
cards.misconception: VPC firewall rules support TCP source-port filters.

cards.statement: A hierarchical firewall policy associated with a folder automatically applies to its descendant projects.
cards.explanation: Associating a hierarchical firewall policy with a folder applies its enabled rules to applicable VMs in projects beneath that folder.

cards.statement: Cloud Router exchanges BGP routes over an HA VPN tunnel.
cards.explanation: Cloud Router establishes BGP sessions over HA VPN tunnels to exchange dynamic routes with a peer network.

cards.statement: Cloud Interconnect encrypts VLAN attachment traffic by default.
cards.explanation: Cloud Interconnect does not encrypt traffic by default. HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect is an option for encrypting VLAN attachment traffic.
cards.misconception: A private Interconnect connection provides encryption by default.

cards.statement: A regional internal Application Load Balancer sends traffic to backends in several regions.
cards.explanation: A regional internal Application Load Balancer uses backends in its own region. Cross-region internal mode supports backends across regions.
cards.misconception: Regional internal load balancing distributes requests to multi-region backends.

cards.statement: Premium Tier brings internet traffic onto Google's global network near the client.
cards.explanation: With Premium Tier, incoming traffic enters Google's network at a point of presence close to the sender and travels across Google's network toward the resource.

cards.statement: Deleting a Config Connector object from the cluster deletes its Google Cloud resource by default.
cards.explanation: Once Config Connector manages a resource, deleting its Kubernetes object deletes the resource too, unless the object has the cnrm.cloud.google.com/deletion-policy: abandon annotation.

cards.statement: Infrastructure Manager deploys Google Cloud resources from Deployment Manager templates.
cards.explanation: Infrastructure Manager deploys Terraform configurations. Deployment Manager used YAML configurations and Jinja or Python templates and has reached end of support.
cards.misconception: Infrastructure Manager accepts Deployment Manager templates as its deployment format.

cards.statement: Artifact Registry stores Helm charts as OCI artifacts in Docker-format repositories.
cards.explanation: Helm 3.8.0 or later pushes charts in OCI format to an Artifact Registry Docker repository, and Helm can then install a chart from that repository as a release.

source.title: Store Helm charts in Artifact Registry

cards.statement: Application Design Center lets developers add components while instantiating a standard template.
cards.explanation: When developers create an application from an Application Design Center standard template, they can configure its components but cannot add or remove them.
cards.misconception: Developers can change a standard template's component set when creating an application.
cards.volatilityNote: Application Design Center template capabilities continue to evolve.

cards.statement: Teams register Application Design Center deployments in App Hub as a separate manual step.
cards.explanation: When you deploy an application with Application Design Center, it registers the application in App Hub automatically.
cards.misconception: Deployed Application Design Center apps need manual App Hub registration.

cards.statement: Gemini CLI is available by default in Cloud Shell for terminal-based development work.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud provides Gemini CLI in Cloud Shell with no additional installation step.
cards.volatilityNote: Availability of AI tooling in Cloud Shell can change.

cards.statement: With a Gemini Code Assist edition, Gemini CLI gets a quota apart from Gemini Code Assist agent mode.
cards.explanation: Each Gemini Code Assist edition grants quotas that Gemini CLI shares with Gemini Code Assist agent mode; a Gemini API key is a separate pay-as-you-go option.
cards.misconception: Gemini CLI has a request pool independent of Code Assist agent mode.

cards.statement: Google Antigravity's visual artifacts can include browser recordings alongside code diffs.
cards.explanation: Google Antigravity uses visual artifacts, including plans, code diffs, and browser recordings, to show and verify agent work.
cards.volatilityNote: Google Antigravity's agent reporting features can change.

cards.statement: Gemini Cloud Assist can refine Terraform infrastructure code through chat prompts.
cards.explanation: Gemini Cloud Assist supports interactive generation and refinement of Terraform code for Google Cloud infrastructure.
cards.volatilityNote: Gemini Cloud Assist is a Preview offering.

cards.statement: By default, Compute Engine keeps snapshots from a snapshot schedule after their source disk is deleted.
cards.explanation: When a source disk is deleted, snapshots made by its schedule are retained until you delete them, unless you set the schedule so its retention policy keeps applying.

cards.statement: A Compute Engine machine image captures the source VM's memory state.
cards.explanation: A Compute Engine machine image captures VM configuration and disk data, but not data held in the VM's memory.
cards.misconception: Machine images preserve a running VM's RAM contents.

cards.statement: GKE cluster autoscaler resizes node pools according to the resource requests that Pods declare.
cards.explanation: Cluster autoscaler bases its decisions on Pod resource requests rather than actual utilization, adding nodes when Pods can't be scheduled and removing underused ones.

cards.statement: GKE Autopilot supplies default resource requests for Pod containers that omit them.
cards.explanation: GKE Autopilot fills in missing Pod container resource requests using defaults for the selected compute configuration.
cards.volatilityNote: GKE Autopilot request defaults can vary by version and compute class.

cards.statement: Manually upgrading a GKE Standard node pool upgrades the cluster's other pools at the same time.
cards.explanation: GKE Standard node pools can be upgraded independently, so a manual upgrade of one pool does not upgrade the other pools.
cards.misconception: A manual GKE node pool upgrade is a cluster-wide node upgrade.

cards.statement: Cloud Run can split service traffic among revisions by percentage.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run traffic settings assign percentages to service revisions, enabling gradual rollouts and rollbacks.

source.title: Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration

cards.statement: Cloud Run waits for a new revision deployment before applying a service-level maximum instances change.
cards.explanation: A change to a service-level maximum instances setting takes effect immediately and caps the instances of the whole service, with no new revision deployment needed.
cards.misconception: A revision-level maximum instance setting limits the combined instances of a service.

cards.statement: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform lists deployed agents across an organization.
cards.explanation: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform lists deployed agents for a specified Google Cloud project and location.
cards.misconception: One Agent Runtime listing spans an entire organization.
tags: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
cards.volatilityNote: Agent Runtime management interfaces and product branding can change.

cards.statement: Cloud Workstations retains its runtime VM after a user session ends.
cards.explanation: Cloud Workstations deletes the runtime VM when a session ends. It detaches and retains the persistent home disk for later sessions.
cards.misconception: A stopped workstation keeps its runtime VM for the next session.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage uniform bucket-level access uses IAM for object access instead of ACLs.
cards.explanation: Enabling uniform bucket-level access disables bucket and object ACLs, leaving IAM to grant access to objects in the bucket.

cards.statement: Cloud SQL for MySQL uses binary logs to support point-in-time recovery.
cards.explanation: Cloud SQL for MySQL enables binary logging for point-in-time recovery, allowing restoration to a chosen point within the retained log window.

cards.statement: Firestore backup schedules write backups to a Cloud Storage bucket that the user selects.
cards.explanation: Firestore scheduled backups are managed backup resources that reside in the same location as their source database; the user does not select a Cloud Storage bucket.
cards.misconception: Firestore scheduled backups use a user-chosen Cloud Storage destination.

cards.statement: A Bigtable backup passes through Cloud Storage when restored to a different instance.
cards.explanation: Bigtable restores its managed backups directly into a table, including in a different instance; no Cloud Storage export or import is needed.
cards.misconception: Cross-instance Bigtable recovery needs a Cloud Storage staging step.

cards.statement: Database Center reports real-time health data for a database fleet.
cards.explanation: Database Center summarizes fleet health issues, but its displayed data is not real-time and can take time to update.
cards.misconception: Database Center health findings update instantly with database state.
cards.volatilityNote: Database Center data freshness and dashboard behavior can change.

cards.statement: Rewriting a Nearline object to Coldline within 30 days can incur an early deletion charge.
cards.explanation: A storage class change by rewrite replaces the object, so Nearline's 30-day minimum storage duration is billed. Class changes by Object Lifecycle Management or Autoclass are exempt.

cards.statement: A Cloud Storage regional bucket uses a CMEK key ring in that same region.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage requires a Cloud KMS key ring used for customer-managed encryption to match the location of the bucket's data.

cards.statement: AlloyDB continuous backup can restore a cluster directly into another region.
cards.explanation: AlloyDB continuous backup creates a recovered cluster in the same region as its source cluster.
cards.misconception: AlloyDB point-in-time recovery directly creates a cluster in a different region.

cards.statement: A Spanner backup keeps its original expiration date after creation.
cards.explanation: Spanner lets an operator update an existing backup's expiration date using the console or gcloud spanner backups update-metadata.
cards.misconception: A Spanner backup's retention endpoint is immutable.

cards.statement: An administrator can expand a subnet's primary IPv4 range after creating the subnet.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud permits expansion of a subnet's primary IPv4 range after creation if the larger range does not overlap conflicting ranges.

cards.statement: A subnet's secondary IPv4 range can be replaced while instances still use addresses from it.
cards.explanation: A subnet's secondary IPv4 range can be removed or replaced only when no instances use that range.
cards.misconception: Instances can keep using a secondary range while it is replaced.

cards.statement: A running VM keeps its current external IPv4 address when you promote that ephemeral address to a static one.
cards.explanation: Promoting an in-use ephemeral external IP address to static keeps the address and drops no packets. The reservation then outlives the VM until you release it.

source.title: Reserve a static external IP address

cards.statement: A reserved static internal IPv4 address can be assigned to a VM in another subnet of the same VPC.
cards.explanation: A static internal IPv4 address belongs to the subnet chosen for its reservation and comes from that subnet's primary range.
cards.misconception: An internal static IP reservation can move between subnets in one VPC.

source.title: Reserve a static internal IP address

cards.statement: A custom static route can name a Compute Engine VM in its VPC network as a next hop.
cards.explanation: A custom static route can name a VM as its next hop when that VM has an interface in the route's VPC network.

cards.statement: Among eligible custom static routes to one destination, a larger priority number takes precedence.
cards.explanation: For eligible custom static routes to the same destination, a smaller priority number has higher priority.
cards.misconception: Larger numeric route priority values win.

cards.statement: A Cloud DNS private zone answers queries from any VPC network in its organization.
cards.explanation: A Cloud DNS private zone answers queries from VPC networks that are authorized for that zone, rather than from the whole organization.
cards.misconception: Private DNS visibility follows organization membership.

cards.statement: One Cloud NAT gateway can serve subnets in several regions of the same VPC network.
cards.explanation: A Cloud NAT gateway is regional and serves configured subnets in that region. Another region needs another gateway.
cards.misconception: One Cloud NAT gateway spans regions.

cards.statement: VPC firewall rules logging records each packet in an allowed TCP connection.
cards.explanation: VPC firewall rules logging records an allowed TCP connection once, rather than recording every packet in that connection.
cards.misconception: Firewall rule logging captures each packet of an allowed connection.

cards.statement: Each Cloud NGFW firewall policy rule has a unique priority within its policy.
cards.explanation: Cloud NGFW requires distinct priority numbers for rules within the same firewall policy, making their evaluation order clear.

cards.statement: Engineers define log-based metrics by calling the Cloud Monitoring API to create the metric.
cards.explanation: Log-based metrics are user-defined metrics, but the Cloud Monitoring API can't create them. You define them in Cloud Logging, which creates the metric and sends its data to Cloud Monitoring.
cards.misconception: Every user-defined metric, including log-based ones, is created with the Cloud Monitoring API.

source.title: Create user-defined metrics with the API

cards.statement: Data Access audit logs are enabled by default for Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage need explicit enablement. BigQuery is the default-enabled exception.
cards.misconception: Cloud Storage Data Access logging is on by default.

cards.statement: A Cloud Logging sink can route matching log entries to a BigQuery dataset.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Logging sink filters log entries and can route matches to a write-enabled BigQuery dataset.

cards.statement: Cloud Logging lets you set a custom retention period for a user-defined log bucket.
cards.explanation: User-defined Cloud Logging buckets support a configured retention period that determines how long stored entries remain available.

cards.statement: The Ops Agent merges its config.yaml settings with its built-in configuration when it restarts.
cards.explanation: User settings in config.yaml are merged with the built-in configuration on restart; to override a built-in receiver, processor or pipeline, redefine it with the same identifier.

cards.statement: Managed collection in Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes GKE Pods from outside the cluster.
cards.explanation: Managed collection runs Prometheus-based collectors inside the cluster; they scrape local targets and push metrics to Google's datastore.
cards.misconception: Google's central service scrapes GKE Pods remotely.
tags: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

cards.statement: Personalized Service Health rates each incident's relevance to a selected project, such as Impacted or Related.
cards.explanation: For the selected project, the Service Health dashboard labels Google Cloud incidents Impacted, Related, Partially Related, Not Impacted or Unknown, showing how each one affects that project.

source.title: Quickstart: View service health events in the Google Cloud console

cards.statement: Active Assist automatically applies recommendations as soon as they appear in the Google Cloud console.
cards.explanation: Active Assist presents recommendations for review; an authorized user applies or dismisses them.
cards.misconception: Active Assist auto-remediates each recommendation when it appears.

cards.statement: Cloud Hub limits its active Google Cloud incident views to individual projects.
cards.explanation: Cloud Hub shows active Google Cloud incidents for a selected project or an App Hub application.
cards.misconception: Cloud Hub cannot display incidents in an application view.
cards.volatilityNote: Cloud Hub's operations views can evolve.

cards.statement: A single IAM role binding names one role and can list several principals who receive that role.
cards.explanation: Each role binding in an allow policy binds one or more principals to exactly one IAM role, so granting those principals a second role takes another binding.

cards.statement: gcloud projects set-iam-policy merges a policy file into the project's allow policy.
cards.explanation: Setting an allow policy overwrites the existing one, so bindings missing from the file are removed; gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding grants one role and keeps the rest.
cards.misconception: set-iam-policy adds to the current policy instead of replacing it.

source.title: Manage access to projects, folders, and organizations

cards.statement: A project admin can remove an inherited IAM role by editing the project's allow policy.
cards.explanation: To edit an inherited IAM grant, change the allow policy on the resource where the role was granted, such as a parent folder.
cards.misconception: A child project's policy can remove a parent grant.

source.title: Manage access to projects, folders, and organizations

cards.statement: IAM predefined roles retain the same permission set when Google adds service features.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud manages predefined roles and can update their permissions as services evolve.
cards.misconception: Predefined role permissions remain fixed.

cards.statement: Folders are valid creation scopes for IAM custom roles.
cards.explanation: IAM custom roles are created in an organization or project, not directly in a folder.
cards.misconception: An IAM custom role can be defined on a folder.

cards.statement: A project-level IAM custom role accepts folder administration permissions.
cards.explanation: A project-level IAM custom role cannot include permissions usable only at the folder or organization level.
cards.misconception: Project custom roles can include parent-resource permissions.

cards.statement: An IAM deny policy can block a permission granted by an allow policy.
cards.explanation: IAM evaluates relevant deny policies before allow policies, so a deny rule can override a role grant for a supported permission.

cards.statement: IAM Conditions can limit a role grant using the request time.
cards.explanation: An IAM Condition can evaluate request.time to make a role binding apply during a specified period.

cards.statement: Conditional IAM role bindings use version 3 of the allow-policy schema.
cards.explanation: Version 3 of an IAM allow policy represents conditional role bindings; version 1 omits their conditions.

cards.statement: A user-managed service account remains in the project where it was created.
cards.explanation: Each service account is located in one project and cannot be moved to another project after creation.

cards.statement: A project administrator creates and manages service agents used by Google Cloud services.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud creates and manages service agents so its services can access resources on a customer's behalf.
cards.misconception: Project administrators manage service agents like user-managed accounts.

cards.statement: Access scopes on a VM can further limit API calls made with its attached service account.
cards.explanation: An app on the VM needs both IAM roles on the service account and matching access scopes. Google recommends the cloud-platform scope and controlling access with IAM roles.

cards.statement: An IAM role granted on a service account controls which resources that account can access.
cards.explanation: Roles granted on a service account resource control who may use or manage that account. Grants to the account on other resources control what it can access.
cards.misconception: The service account's own allow policy controls its outgoing resource access.

cards.statement: The Service Account User role provides the permission to attach a service account to a VM.
cards.explanation: Service Account User includes iam.serviceAccounts.actAs, the permission needed to attach a service account to a VM.

cards.statement: gcloud impersonation of a service account reads its downloaded private key.
cards.explanation: gcloud impersonation generates short-lived credentials for the target service account instead of using its downloaded key.
cards.misconception: gcloud impersonation requires a target service account key file.

cards.statement: Google rotates user-managed service account keys after they are downloaded.
cards.explanation: Users manage rotation of their user-managed service account keys by replacing old keys and invalidating them.
cards.misconception: Google rotates downloaded service account keys.

source.title: Best practices for managing service account keys

cards.statement: Workload Identity Federation for GKE can grant a Kubernetes ServiceAccount direct IAM access to a resource.
cards.explanation: GKE workloads can receive IAM grants as principals representing Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, so direct access does not require an IAM service account.

source.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE

cards.statement: GKE Pods using Workload Identity Federation for GKE obtain tokens from the Compute Engine metadata server.
cards.explanation: The GKE metadata server intercepts token requests from Pods using Workload Identity Federation for GKE and returns the credentials.
cards.misconception: GKE Pods still fetch workload tokens from the Compute Engine metadata server.

source.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE
